Social Media and Self-Image.q: In media analysis, “biased language” means words that …
o: show caution and uncertainty about a claim
show a strong opinion and are not fair
state facts with full and clear evidence
ask a question that needs no answer
Social Media and Self-Image.e: The lesson defines biased language as words that show a strong opinion and are not fair or neutral.

o: judging yourself by comparing with others
using adjectives that express a judgment
sharing every ordinary detail of your day
posting only your best moments online
Social Media and Self-Image.e: It is the tendency to post only the best moments online, creating a false image of reality.

Social Media and Self-Image.q: Which word is a hedging word?
o: might
always
extremely
never
Social Media and Self-Image.e: Hedging words such as may, might and could show uncertainty or caution.

Social Media and Self-Image.q: In the sentence “It was an extremely unfair post”, the word “extremely” is …
o: a hedging word
an absolute word
a rhetorical question
an intensifier
Social Media and Self-Image.e: Intensifiers such as very, extremely and significantly make ideas stronger.

Social Media and Self-Image.q: Which sentence uses neutral, hedging language?
o: Some studies suggest social media may affect self-esteem.
Social media totally destroys every teenager’s confidence.
All teenagers believe everything they read online, always.
Social media is the worst thing that ever happened to us.
Social Media and Self-Image.e: Neutral language is balanced; “some studies suggest” and “may” avoid absolute claims.

Social Media and Self-Image.q: What is the main effect of a rhetorical question such as “Do I really need this?”
o: It shows the writer is unsure.
It gives detailed evidence.
It makes the reader think.
It states a fact with confidence.
Social Media and Self-Image.e: Rhetorical questions do not need an answer; they are used to make the reader think.

Exploring Modern Lifestyles.q: How much physical activity do health experts recommend for teenagers every day?
o: at least 20 minutes of light walking only
at least 90 minutes of hard, competitive team sports
at least 30 minutes of slow stretching
at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-hard activity
Exploring Modern Lifestyles.e: The text says teenagers should do at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-hard physical activity every day.

Exploring Modern Lifestyles.q: According to the text, endorphins released during exercise …
o: reduce stress and boost mood
make teenagers sleep less
increase feelings of anxiety
replace the need for a good diet
Exploring Modern Lifestyles.e: Physical activity releases endorphins, chemicals that reduce stress and anxiety while boosting mood and self-confidence.

Exploring Modern Lifestyles.q: According to the text, more than 80% of teenagers worldwide fail to meet the daily activity target mainly because of …
o: a dislike of competitive sport
sedentary screen-based habits
sleeping too many hours a night
heavy homework from their schools
Exploring Modern Lifestyles.e: The WHO-led study links the failure “largely” to sedentary screen-based habits; the text does not blame sport, sleep or homework.

Exploring Modern Lifestyles.q: Salma sleeps only six hours a night because she uses her phone in bed. Which advice from the text would help her most?
o: Drink a high-caffeine drink at night.
Avoid screens for an hour before bed.
Keep studying late so she feels tired.
Replace sleep with mindfulness practice.
Exploring Modern Lifestyles.e: The text says avoiding screens for one hour before sleeping improves sleep quality; teenagers need eight to ten hours a night.

Exploring Modern Lifestyles.q: Which of these is a sedentary habit?
o: cycling to school every day
gaming for hours
swimming laps after class
a brisk walk in the park
Exploring Modern Lifestyles.e: Sedentary means involving little physical movement; cycling, swimming and brisk walking all count towards the daily activity target.

Exploring Modern Lifestyles.q: Complete: “Adolescents ……… sleep fewer than seven hours are more likely to report anxiety.”
o: which
whose
where
who
Exploring Modern Lifestyles.e: We use the relative pronoun “who” to add information about people.

Whose Responsibility Is It?.q: What does having an “internal locus of control” mean?
o: believing outside forces decide your life
believing that the government controls your health
believing that luck shapes every result
believing your own actions decide outcomes
Whose Responsibility Is It?.e: It is the belief that one’s own actions, rather than external forces, determine outcomes.

Whose Responsibility Is It?.q: In the article, the word “agency” means …
o: a company that sells products
an obstacle that limits choice
the capacity to choose and act
a gentle push towards a behavior
Whose Responsibility Is It?.e: The text defines agency as the capacity to choose and act.

Whose Responsibility Is It?.q: Ali wants to exercise, but his neighborhood has no safe parks and the sports club is too expensive. The article would call this …
o: a failure of willpower
a structural barrier
an internal locus of control
a nudge from the government
Whose Responsibility Is It?.e: Structural barriers are obstacles in the environment that restrict genuine choice; the article says they are not failures of willpower.

Whose Responsibility Is It?.q: A school canteen puts fruit at eye level and snacks on a lower shelf, but students can still buy either. This is an example of …
o: a nudge
a structural barrier
a strict ban on junk food
disempowering students
Whose Responsibility Is It?.e: A nudge is a small change to the context that shifts behavior without restricting freedom; nothing is banned here.

Whose Responsibility Is It?.q: Why do supporters of personal responsibility warn against blaming outside forces for every choice?
o: Governments will raise taxes.
People may become passive.
Advertising will become illegal.
Families will stop eating together.
Whose Responsibility Is It?.e: The article says that when people blame outside forces entirely, “they risk becoming passive”; taking ownership builds confidence and resilience.

Whose Responsibility Is It?.q: According to supporters, why do policies such as taxes on high-sugar drinks not remove individual freedom?
o: They force everyone to exercise daily.
They make the healthy choice easier.
They let companies decide what we eat.
They remove all advertising for snacks.
Whose Responsibility Is It?.e: Supporters say these measures reshape the environment so that the healthier choice becomes the easier one, while people can still choose.

Understanding Mental Health.q: Which sentence is a first conditional?
o: If schools offered counseling, stress would fall.
If schools had offered help, stress would have fallen.
If schools offer counseling, stress may fall.
If schools offer counseling, stress would have fallen.
Understanding Mental Health.e: The first conditional (real) uses If + present simple, then will/may + verb.

Understanding Mental Health.q: Complete: “If social media were less popular, teenagers ……… less pressure.”
o: will feel
would have felt
would feel
had felt
Understanding Mental Health.e: This is a second conditional (hypothetical): If + past simple, would + verb.

Understanding Mental Health.q: Complete: “If the study had included more schools, the findings ……… more conclusive.”
o: will be
would have been
would have being
has been
Understanding Mental Health.e: The third conditional uses If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

Understanding Mental Health.q: The third conditional is used to talk about …
o: a real future possibility
a general scientific fact
a habit in the present
an unreal past situation
Understanding Mental Health.e: The book calls the third conditional “unreal past”, e.g. If the study had included more schools…

Understanding Mental Health.q: Why are conditional structures useful in academic writing, according to the lesson?
o: They make every single claim sound fully and totally certain.
They express certainty, possibility, or caution.
They replace the need for any evidence.
They are used only to tell personal stories.
Understanding Mental Health.e: Conditionals help writers hedge, expressing certainty, possibility, or caution when making claims based on evidence.

Understanding Mental Health.q: “If more schools offered counseling, students would most likely feel better supported.” The writer uses the second conditional because the situation is …
o: imagined, not true at present
a completed event in the distant past
a general scientific fact about stress
a definite plan for the coming week
Understanding Mental Health.e: The book calls the second conditional hypothetical: If + past simple, would + verb describes an imagined present or future situation.

Screen Time and Young People.q: In the lesson’s True/False task, “Teenagers spend an average of seven hours on screens, including school screen time” is marked False. Why?
o: The real average is closer to ten hours.
The figure only counts gaming on phones.
The figure applies to adults, not teenagers.
The figure excludes school screen time.
Screen Time and Young People.e: The book’s justification says the seven-hour figure excludes school screen time, so “including school screen time” makes the statement false.

o: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
Use screens for only 20 minutes, about 20 times each week.
Take a 20-minute break after every 20 messages.
Sleep 20 minutes after using a screen for 20 hours.
Screen Time and Young People.e: Experts recommend looking at something 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds every 20 minutes.

Screen Time and Young People.q: Mona never uses her phone at dinner or after 10 p.m. She has set clear …
o: withdrawals
interferences
anxieties
boundaries
Screen Time and Young People.e: Boundaries are limits or rules that show what is acceptable or allowed, such as avoiding phones before bed.

Screen Time and Young People.q: Omar plans to play a game for ten minutes, but he can’t stop and plays for three hours every night. The game seems to be …
o: fulfilling
addictive
structured
beneficial
Screen Time and Young People.e: Addictive means causing a very strong need to keep doing or using something, like being unable to stop playing.

Screen Time and Young People.q: “Using phones late at night can interfere with sleep.” This means that phones can …
o: affect sleep in a negative way
help people fall asleep more quickly
replace the need for sleep completely
make no difference to sleep at all
Screen Time and Young People.e: To interfere is to affect a situation negatively or stop something from working properly.

Screen Time and Young People.q: According to the comparison table, what can Egypt learn from Finland?
o: to provide mental health education
to balance screens with nature
to ban social media for teenagers
to build more gaming centers
Screen Time and Young People.e: Finland has less screen time and more outdoor activities, so Egypt can learn to balance screens with nature.

Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.q: What do psychologists call the state of complete absorption in a meaningful task?
o: anxiety
withdrawal
flow
rehearsal
Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.e: The article says psychologists call this state “flow”.

Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.q: According to the article, thirty minutes of creative activity a day can …
o: replace the need for sleep and exercise
increase screen time safely
raise levels of cortisol
reduce the stress hormone cortisol
Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.e: Research suggests thirty minutes of creative engagement daily can measurably reduce the stress hormone cortisol.

Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.q: How is creative activity different from passive screen entertainment?
o: It needs no thinking, planning or effort at all.
The brain must produce, not just consume.
It always has one single correct answer.
It is mostly done alone and in silence.
Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.e: Creative activity demands that the brain produce rather than merely consume.

Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.q: Complete: “She enjoys ……… in her free time.”
o: to painting
paint
painted
painting
Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.e: “Enjoy” is followed by a gerund (verb + ing).

Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.q: Complete: “On his way home, Omar stopped ……… his mom her favorite magazine.”
o: buying
to buy
buy
to buying
Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.e: “Stop + to-infinitive” means stopping one action in order to do another (purpose).

Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.q: What does “Try eating more vegetables” mean?
o: Make a big effort to eat more.
Eat more and see if it helps.
Stop eating vegetables at once.
Remember that you ate them.
Creative Arts as Leisure Activities.e: Try + gerund means do something to see if it helps; try + to-infinitive means make an effort.

Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.q: According to the lesson, what has created a “movement crisis” among young people?
o: the high cost of sports shoes
too many compulsory sports lessons at school
screen time and academic pressure
a lack of interest from parents
Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.e: The lesson states that screen time and academic pressure have created a “movement crisis”.

Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.q: In the Benefits of Sports Pyramid, which belongs to the physical foundation?
o: teamwork and leadership
cardiovascular fitness
self-esteem
belonging
Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.e: The physical foundation includes cardiovascular fitness, strength, coordination, endurance and healthy weight.

Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.q: Choose the correct word: “Sport has a ……… impact on teenagers’ mental health.”
o: significance
signify
significantly
significant
Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.e: An adjective is needed before the noun “impact”.

Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.q: Choose the correct word: “Many students do not ……… in any physical activity.”
o: participation
participate
participant
participating
Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.e: After “do not” we need the base form of the verb.

Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.q: “The game was played competitively.” What does this tell us about the game?
o: Nobody cared about the result.
The players were all beginners.
Both teams tried hard to win.
It was cancelled before the end.
Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.e: Competitively is an adverb describing how the game was played: with both teams trying their best to win.

Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.q: Correct the word-form error: “The increasing popular of social media has changed communication.”
o: popularly
popularize
unpopularly
popularity
Sport and Physical Activity as Leisure.e: After “the increasing” we need a noun, so “popular” becomes “popularity”.

Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.q: At the start of the extract, what was the narrator’s idea of leisure?
o: staying at home and doing nothing
cycling long distances with friends
swimming in the sea every weekend
travelling to new cities alone
Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.e: He believed the best free day was spent at home watching a series and doing absolutely nothing.

Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.q: What stopped the narrator from giving up during the trip?
o: a sudden storm and rain
a phone call from his worried family
his pride and curiosity
a broken bicycle chain
Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.e: Pride, and curiosity about whether he could finish, kept him going.

Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.q: Complete: “As the afternoon ………, the heat became increasingly difficult to bear.”
o: insisted
struggled to keep up
gave in
wore on
Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.e: “Wore on” means passed gradually and is used of time, so it fits “the afternoon”; the other options cannot describe time passing.

Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.q: The friend kept cycling “as if the heat were simply decoration.” This suggests that the friend …
o: was hardly bothered by the heat
wanted to decorate his bicycle for the trip
was suffering more than the narrator did
was the one who wanted to call a taxi
Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.e: The comparison shows the experienced friend was not troubled by the heat, while the narrator struggled and thought of calling a taxi.

Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.q: Complete: “When we finally stopped, I realized we ……… much farther than I had expected.”
o: have cycled
had cycled
cycle
are cycling
Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.e: The past perfect shows an action completed before another past action (realized).

Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.q: What did the trip teach the narrator about leisure?
o: It can come from effort, not just comfort.
It must always mean resting at home.
It is only enjoyable with expensive equipment.
It should be avoided when the sun is strong.
Not Exactly a Relaxing Day.e: He learned that leisure is not always about comfort; the best moments can come from effort.

Consolidation Review A.q: “A mindful student thinks before sharing photos online.” The opposite of “mindful” is …
o: careless
attentive
aware
thoughtful
Consolidation Review A.e: Mindful means paying careful attention, so its opposite is careless.

o: She suggested taking a short break.
She suggested to take a short break.
She suggested take a short break.
She suggested took a short break.
Consolidation Review A.e: “Suggest” is followed by a gerund (verb + ing).

o: By the time we arrived there, the sun has already risen.
By the time we arrived, the sun had already rose.
By the time we arrived, the sun had already risen.
By the time we arrived, the sun was already rise.
Consolidation Review A.e: The past perfect (had + past participle “risen”) shows the earlier past action.

Consolidation Review A.q: In the reading text, why did Nadia first feel dissatisfied with her life?
o: Her friends stopped spending time with her.
She studied every weekend instead of going out.
She compared it with perfect-looking posts.
She wanted to be a famous photographer.
Consolidation Review A.e: Nadia checked popular accounts every morning and felt her own life was ordinary compared with them.

Consolidation Review A.q: What does Nadia’s edited café photo show about social media users?
o: They share every difficult detail of their day.
They may make experiences look better.
They never change photos before posting them.
They describe ordinary moments exactly as they are.
Consolidation Review A.e: Nadia changed the light and made the café look more expensive, presenting the afternoon as better than it really was.

Consolidation Review A.q: What did Nadia join when she reduced the time she spent on her phone?
o: a photography competition
a popular online account
a weekend sports team
a school art club
Consolidation Review A.e: The text says she reduced her phone time, joined a school art club and began meeting Jana for walks on weekends.

Sites of Memory.q: The speaker calls Karnak “a landscape of accumulated memory.” Here “accumulated” means memory that has been …
o: built up over time
carved into one wall
forgotten by most people
removed from the site
Sites of Memory.e: Accumulated means built up gradually over time; Karnak was developed during the reigns of many pharaohs.

Sites of Memory.q: A ram-headed sphinx is an ancient Egyptian statue with …
o: a ram’s body and a lion’s head
a human’s body and a ram’s head
a lion’s body and a human head
a lion’s body and a ram’s head
Sites of Memory.e: The vocabulary list defines it as a statue with a lion’s body and a ram’s head.

Sites of Memory.q: Choose the correct preposition: “Visitors walk ……… the avenue of sphinxes.”
o: along
during
since
for
Sites of Memory.e: “Along” is used with a linear space, such as an avenue.

Sites of Memory.q: Choose the correct preposition: “Karnak was developed ……… the reigns of many pharaohs.”
o: during
along
at
in front of
Sites of Memory.e: “During” is used with a period of time, such as a reign.

Sites of Memory.q: According to the unit timeline, what happened in 1822 AD?
o: Narmer united Upper and Lower Egypt.
Alexander the Great founded the city of Alexandria.
The Egyptian Museum opened in Cairo.
Champollion deciphered the Rosetta Stone.
Sites of Memory.e: In 1822 Champollion deciphered the Rosetta Stone, so ancient Egyptian writing was finally understood.

Sites of Memory.q: In the lesson’s True/False example, why is “The speaker visited Karnak to avoid the crowds” marked Not Given?
o: The speaker arrived in the afternoon.
The speaker says there were no crowds.
The recording never says why.
The speaker went with a tour group.
Sites of Memory.e: The recording says the visit was early, “before the tour groups arrive”, but gives no reason, so the statement is Not Given.

The Museum as a Storyteller.q: When did the Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) open to the public?
o: 4 November 1902
4 November 2025
14 October 2025
the first of January 2003
The Museum as a Storyteller.e: The article states the GEM opened its doors to the public on 4 November 2025.

o: Despite the GEM is huge, visitors find their way easily.
Although the GEM is huge, visitors find their way easily.
Although its huge size, visitors find their way easily.
In spite of the GEM is huge, visitors find their way easily.
The Museum as a Storyteller.e: “Although” is followed by a clause; “despite” and “in spite of” must be followed by a noun phrase, not a clause.

The Museum as a Storyteller.q: Which statement about the GEM is FALSE, according to the article?
o: Tutankhamun’s full collection was shown before.
It holds more than 100,000 ancient Egyptian artifacts.
Its Grand Staircase displays 87 colossal royal statues.
It contains laboratories for conservation work.
The Museum as a Storyteller.e: The complete Tutankhamun collection is displayed together “for the first time in history”; the other three statements are true.

The Museum as a Storyteller.q: Choose the correct word: “……… its modern design, the GEM places ancient history at its heart.”
o: Despite
Although
Even though
While
The Museum as a Storyteller.e: “Despite” is followed by a noun phrase; although, even though and while need a clause.

The Museum as a Storyteller.q: According to the article, how is the GEM different from many museums?
o: It is designed mainly for foreign tourists.
It displays only royal and temple objects.
It has an educational role for students.
It tells every story from Egypt’s past.
The Museum as a Storyteller.e: Unlike museums designed mainly for tourists, the GEM educates Egyptian students; it also shows everyday objects but cannot tell every story.

o: people who visit museums as foreign tourists
people who organize a museum’s contents
people who dig to find old objects
people who sell copies of artifacts
The Museum as a Storyteller.e: Curators look after and organize the contents of a museum or exhibition.

o: spread rapidly and widely online
be checked carefully by historians
be deleted from social media
be stored in a digital archive
The Viral Past.e: To go viral means to spread rapidly and widely online, often within 24 hours.

The Viral Past.q: Hana sees a viral post about ancient Alexandria with no source and no date. Following the writer’s advice, what should she do first?
o: Share it before it is deleted.
Check its source and date.
Trust it because it has many likes.
Add a colorized photo to it.
The Viral Past.e: Media literacy means questioning sources, checking dates and consulting multiple perspectives; popularity has no real relationship to truth.

The Viral Past.q: What point does the writer make with the Great Pyramid example?
o: The pyramid was built in just one decade.
Emotional posts are usually accurate ones.
Historians share facts far too slowly.
A viral claim can be completely false.
The Viral Past.e: The post claimed one decade, but construction took decades and tens of thousands of workers: wide spread says nothing about truth.

The Viral Past.q: What solution does the writer propose to historical misinformation?
o: banning all old photos
media literacy
deleting viral posts
colorizing old images
The Viral Past.e: Media literacy means questioning sources, checking dates and consulting multiple perspectives.

The Viral Past.q: “Rarely do virality and accuracy move in the same direction.” What does the writer mean?
o: Accurate posts always go viral quickly.
Viral posts are often inaccurate.
Viral posts are checked by historians.
Old photos never spread on social media.
The Viral Past.e: What spreads widely is seldom what is accurate, because platforms are designed to promote engagement, not accuracy.

The Viral Past.q: In the post “Share before this gets deleted!”, which unreliable feature is used?
o: hedging language
neutral language
urgency signals
careful evidence
The Viral Past.e: Urgency signals create panic or pressure to act immediately.

Social Media and Historical Events.q: What does it mean to “document” a historical event?
o: to forget it as quickly as possible
to change the details of it later
to spread rumors about it online
to create a lasting record of it
Social Media and Historical Events.e: Documenting means creating a lasting record through primary evidence, such as a text, photo, or video.

Social Media and Historical Events.q: “Citizen journalism” is news reporting carried out by …
o: members of the public
trained journalists only
government ministries
academic historians
Social Media and Historical Events.e: Citizen journalism is news reporting by members of the public, not trained journalists.

Social Media and Historical Events.q: A post about a famous museum lists only its masterpieces and says nothing about how the objects got there. This is an example of …
o: real-time documentation
citizen journalism
selective framing
an online digital archive
Social Media and Historical Events.e: Selective framing is choosing which details to include or exclude to shape the audience’s understanding; this post leaves out how the objects arrived.

Social Media and Historical Events.q: Traditionally, documenting history was the job of “official gatekeepers”. Which of these is NOT an official gatekeeper?
o: an official government ministry
a university academic historian
a professional news outlet
a passer-by with a phone
Social Media and Historical Events.e: The lesson names ministries, academic historians and professional news outlets as gatekeepers; a member of the public is a citizen journalist.

Social Media and Historical Events.q: Choose the passive sentence suitable for a formal news report.
o: A royal tomb was discovered in Luxor.
A royal tomb was discovering in Luxor.
A royal tomb was discover in Luxor.
A royal tomb were discovered in Luxor.
Social Media and Historical Events.e: The passive voice is was/were + past participle; “tomb” is singular, so “was discovered”.

Social Media and Historical Events.q: In a news report, why does “In the past, discoveries were reported slowly” belong in the background, not the lead?
o: It does not give what, where and when.
It should be the headline of the report.
It gives the writer’s personal opinion.
It is the most important fact of all.
Social Media and Historical Events.e: The lead must give What + Where + When about the new event; this sentence only gives general background about the past.

Food Waste.q: Which of these is NOT a cause of food waste named in the report?
o: high food prices
buying too much food
storing food incorrectly
confusion about date labels
Food Waste.e: The report names overbuying, poor storage and confusion about date labels; high prices are not mentioned.

Food Waste.q: Mona’s yogurt is one day past its “best before” date, and it looks and smells fine. According to the report, …
o: it is unsafe and must be thrown away.
its “use by” date has also passed.
its quality may have changed.
the shop must give it to a food bank.
Food Waste.e: “Best before” only means taste or quality might change; it does not mean unsafe. The “use by” date is the safety date.

Food Waste.q: Which date tells you when food is no longer safe to eat?
o: best before
packed on
use by
sold on
Food Waste.e: The report explains that the “use by” date tells you when food is no longer safe.

Food Waste.q: What does the report recommend that shops should do?
o: build new refrigeration facilities in homes
give safe leftover food to food banks
raise the price of bread and fruit
stop selling fresh vegetables
Food Waste.e: Shops should be required to give safe leftover food to food banks rather than throw it away.

Food Waste.q: Why does the report say that generosity during Ramadan can sometimes lead to food waste?
o: The report sees generosity as a negative tradition.
Guests usually refuse to eat the food served.
Food prices are much higher during Ramadan.
Poor planning means too much is prepared.
Food Waste.e: The report calls generosity positive and valued, but poor planning can lead to more food being prepared than is eaten.

Food Waste.q: Which sentence uses fronting for emphasis?
o: As a result of poor storage, bread goes bad.
Bread goes bad quickly as a result of poor storage.
Many people throw away food too early.
Shops should give food to food banks.
Food Waste.e: Fronting moves a phrase, here a result phrase, to the beginning of the sentence for emphasis.

Beyond the Brand.q: Why do the biggest companies invest so heavily in brand-building?
o: Brands are cheaper to make than products.
Customers always prefer products without any names.
Governments require every company to do it.
A known brand is worth more than any product.
Beyond the Brand.e: The text says a well-known brand is more valuable than any single product.

Beyond the Brand.q: When brand X puts its tick on a shoe and writes “Just Do It”, what is it really selling?
o: only a comfortable pair of running shoes
the idea that the wearer is stronger
a cheaper product than its competitors
the name of the factory that made it
Beyond the Brand.e: The article says it sells not only shoes but the idea that the wearer is stronger, more determined and ready for a challenge.

Beyond the Brand.q: What did psychologists find when people see the logo of their favorite brand?
o: A brain part linked to identity becomes active.
People stop wanting to buy anything at all.
The brain reacts exactly as to an unknown label.
People feel more stressed and less confident.
Beyond the Brand.e: The part of the brain linked to personal identity becomes more active than with an unknown label.

Beyond the Brand.q: Hana buys expensive branded trainers because they make her feel she belongs, although a cheaper pair is better made. This is …
o: blind brand loyalty
mindful, informed consumption
a structural barrier
loss aversion at a sale
Beyond the Brand.e: Blind brand loyalty means buying based on emotion rather than quality; mindful consumption would mean questioning why she prefers the brand.

Beyond the Brand.q: Complete: “The cake looked delicious, but Ali managed to ……… it because he was on a diet.”
o: prefer
recognize
resist
invest
Beyond the Brand.e: To resist is to stop yourself from doing something; Ali stopped himself from eating the cake.

o: a picture or symbol representing a company
always choosing the same brand
liking one thing more than another
the feeling of being in a group
Beyond the Brand.e: Preference means liking one thing more than another.

Digital Consumption.q: Although social media platforms seem free, what do they actually do?
o: collect information about users
charge users a large monthly fee
delete users’ data after a day
stop users from scrolling
Digital Consumption.e: The lesson says these platforms collect information about users’ behavior and interests.

Digital Consumption.q: Complete: “By the age of 17, the average teenager ……… more time on social media than in school.”
o: has spent
have spent
is spending
spend
Digital Consumption.e: The present perfect (has + past participle) links past time to now; “the average teenager” is singular, so “has spent”.

Digital Consumption.q: “If you are not paying for the product, you are the product.” What does this mean about “free” apps?
o: They will soon start charging users a monthly fee.
They delete all personal data after a day.
They are made only for advertising companies.
They profit from users’ data and attention.
Digital Consumption.e: The lesson says these platforms seem free but collect information about users’ behavior and interests and profit from their attention.

Digital Consumption.q: Why does Team FOR mention infinite scroll and autoplay in the debate?
o: to show apps help people stay connected globally
to show apps are designed to trap users
to show how well apps protect users’ privacy
to show apps give students useful content
Digital Consumption.e: Team FOR argues social media does more harm than good; its notes say apps use infinite scroll and autoplay to trap users online.

Digital Consumption.q: Which sentence best fits paragraph 3 (Negatives) of a review?
o: One of its greatest strengths is its simple design.
A significant drawback is the number of ads.
I would recommend it to students who love art.
ArtNow is a free app designed for young artists.
Digital Consumption.e: Paragraph 3 discusses weaknesses fairly; the other sentences suit the positives, the conclusion and the introduction.

Digital Consumption.q: What should the conclusion of a review include?
o: a list of the product’s technical parts
only the price and where to buy it
the overall judgement and who it suits
a new topic for the next review
Digital Consumption.e: The conclusion summarizes your overall judgement and states who you would recommend it to, and why.

o: fearing a loss more than valuing a gain
buying only what you really need
comparing the prices in many different shops
saving money for a future purchase
Black Friday and Sales Culture.e: Loss aversion is avoiding loss more than gaining; not buying something feels like a loss.

Black Friday and Sales Culture.q: In the jacket example, why does the jacket suddenly feel more attractive?
o: Its quality has suddenly become much better.
Fewer people want to buy it than before.
The brand has become more famous lately.
Not buying it feels like a loss.
Black Friday and Sales Culture.e: This is loss aversion: “If I don’t buy it, I will lose the chance to save 400 pounds,” though nothing is actually lost.

Black Friday and Sales Culture.q: A phrase like “Only 3 left in stock!” is designed to create …
o: a feeling of calm
trust in the famous brand
a feeling of urgency
careful thinking
Black Friday and Sales Culture.e: Such phrases make you feel you must decide immediately or miss the chance.

Black Friday and Sales Culture.q: What did research find about people who shop during sales?
o: They always save a lot of money.
They buy only what they need.
They spend exactly the same.
They spend more money overall.
Black Friday and Sales Culture.e: Sale shoppers actually spend more money overall than people who do not shop during sales.

Black Friday and Sales Culture.q: Complete: “Food waste ……… a bigger problem since 2000.”
o: became
is becoming
has become
have become
Black Friday and Sales Culture.e: The present perfect (has + past participle) is used with “since” + a point in time.

Black Friday and Sales Culture.q: Complete: “The government hasn’t acted on this problem ………”
o: already
since
yet
ever
Black Friday and Sales Culture.e: “Yet” is used with the present perfect in negatives and questions.

Consolidation Review B.q: “A misleading viral post can distort people’s understanding.” “Distort” means …
o: explain it in much greater detail
record it for the very first time
translate it into a different language
change it so it is no longer accurate
Consolidation Review B.e: To distort is to change something so that it is no longer accurate.

Consolidation Review B.q: Complete: “Many supermarkets have not changed their wasteful practices ………”
o: already
yet
since
ever
Consolidation Review B.e: “Yet” is used at the end of negative present perfect sentences.

Consolidation Review B.q: According to “When Places Remember”, why may preserving a historical site not be enough?
o: Old buildings lose their value after many years.
Most visitors prefer screens to real places.
Visitors may need context to understand it.
Sites only have meaning if objects are inside.
Consolidation Review B.e: A ruined building may seem meaningless without context, so the text says “interpretation becomes as important as preservation”.

Consolidation Review B.q: According to “When Places Remember”, whose experiences do many museums now include besides powerful leaders?
o: workers, women and children
only kings and army generals
only major political events
only famous foreign visitors
Consolidation Review B.e: Today many museums also include the experiences of workers, women, children, minority communities and ordinary families.

o: Although the museum is modern, it preserves ancient history.
Despite the museum is very modern, it preserves ancient history.
Although its modern design, it preserves ancient history.
In spite the museum is modern, it preserves ancient history.
Consolidation Review B.e: “Although” is followed by a full clause (subject + verb).

Consolidation Review B.q: According to “When Places Remember”, a place becomes a site of memory when people …
o: rebuild it exactly as it once was long ago
turn it into a modern museum
protect it for its unusual design
link it with meaningful past events
Consolidation Review B.e: A place becomes a site of memory when people connect it with important events, experiences, or individuals.

The Climate Crisis.q: According to scientists, what is the primary driver of the climate crisis?
o: natural sun cycles
ocean currents
human activity
volcanic eruptions
The Climate Crisis.e: Scientists agree human activity, especially burning fossil fuels, is the primary driver of the climate crisis.

o: Because of sea levels are rising, coastal towns are at risk.
Because of rising sea levels, coastal towns are at risk.
Rising sea levels lead to coastal towns are at risk.
Owing to sea levels rise, coastal towns are at risk.
The Climate Crisis.e: “Because of”, “owing to” and “lead to” are followed by a noun phrase, not a clause: “because of rising sea levels”.

The Climate Crisis.q: Why are coral reefs, the “rain forests of the sea”, dying?
o: too many tourists and divers
overfishing and loud noise pollution
ocean warming and acidification
cold water and heavy rain
The Climate Crisis.e: Coral reefs are dying due to ocean warming and acidification, causing mass bleaching.

The Climate Crisis.q: Why does the writer point out that the poorest communities “contribute the least” to climate change?
o: to blame them for causing the crisis
to prove they produce most emissions
to show they are hardly affected at all
to show that the impact is unfair
The Climate Crisis.e: They contribute the least yet are often the hardest hit, which shows that the effects of climate change fall unfairly.

The Climate Crisis.q: Complete: “……… changing rainfall patterns, many fertile regions are becoming dry.”
o: Owing to
Consequently
Since
Leads to
The Climate Crisis.e: “Owing to” is followed by a noun phrase (the cause).

The Climate Crisis.q: “The scientific consensus is clear.” This means that …
o: scientists strongly disagree with each other
one scientist has proved the facts
most scientists agree on the facts
the evidence is still weak and unclear
The Climate Crisis.e: Consensus means general agreement among a group; scientists around the world agree that human activity is the primary driver.

Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.q: What do solar photovoltaic panels do?
o: use the Earth’s heat for power
use moving water to drive turbines
convert sunlight into electricity
harness the energy of the wind
Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.e: Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight into electricity.

o: moving river water
the Earth’s heat
wind power
sunlight
Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.e: In geothermal energy, the Earth’s heat powers turbines.

Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.q: Choose the modal for strong necessity: “Governments ……… invest in clean energy infrastructure now.”
o: might
could
must
may
Solar energy coulds power cities.
Solar energy could powers cities.
Solar energy could powering cities.
Solar energy could power cities.
Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.e: Modal verbs never change form and are followed by the base verb.

Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.q: Which line from the “Green Energy Guide” leaflet is the call to action?
o: “Switch to Solar Today.”
“What is Solar Energy?”
“Solar panels capture sunlight and convert it into electricity.”
“Why are you still paying for energy the sun gives for free?”
Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.e: A call to action asks the reader to do something specific; the others are a subheading, a bullet point and the headline.

Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.q: “Battery storage may solve the problem of intermittency.” What does “may” show here?
o: uncertainty
strong obligation
advice
past ability
Renewable Energy — Powering a Sustainabl.e: The lesson’s modal table says may and might express uncertainty about claims; must shows strong necessity, should gives advice.

o: turning waste into new, useful products
knowing and understanding an issue
using time and resources with very little waste at all
meeting present needs without harming the future
Greening Projects in Egypt.e: Sustainability is the ability to meet present needs without harming future generations.

Greening Projects in Egypt.q: Complete: “The Go Green ……… encourages people to reduce plastic use and recycle waste.”
o: Emissions
Sustainability
Recycling
Initiative
Greening Projects in Egypt.e: An initiative is a plan or program introduced to achieve a specific goal; the lesson names the “Go Green Initiative”.

o: Students recycle regularly plastic bottles.
Students recycle plastic regularly bottles.
Students regularly recycle plastic bottles.
Students do regularly recycling plastic bottles.
Greening Projects in Egypt.e: “Regularly” can go before the main verb (or at the end), but never between the verb and its object.

Greening Projects in Egypt.q: Which word is an adverbial of frequency?
o: regularly
significantly
greatly
largely
Greening Projects in Egypt.e: Adverbials of frequency, like regularly, rarely and frequently, show how often something happens.

Greening Projects in Egypt.q: Which word is an adverbial of degree?
o: rarely
more frequently
regularly
significantly
Greening Projects in Egypt.e: Adverbials of degree, like significantly, greatly and largely, show to what extent.

Greening Projects in Egypt.q: In “Clearly, individual action alone is not enough,” the word “clearly” shows …
o: how often something happens
the writer’s view or attitude
the place where the action happens
the time of the action
Greening Projects in Egypt.e: Certainty/stance adverbials such as clearly and undoubtedly show the writer’s point of view.

Individual and Collective Actions.q: What did Omar Taha’s team design?
o: an electric car for large families
a low-cost solar water heater
a water-cleaning machine
a wind turbine for schools
Individual and Collective Actions.e: Omar said his team had designed a low-cost solar water heater for ordinary rooftops.

Individual and Collective Actions.q: Which detail shows that Omar’s heater is affordable for lower-income families?
o: It was presented at a national conference.
Its materials cost under 3,000 pounds.
It was designed by university students.
It uses energy from the sun.
Individual and Collective Actions.e: Asked about affordability, Omar said the total cost of materials was less than three thousand Egyptian pounds.

Individual and Collective Actions.q: What does Farida’s Nile clean-up campaign mainly show?
o: Only the government can clean the Nile.
Small local efforts can grow big.
The Nile is no longer in any danger.
Big campaigns need no volunteers at all.
Individual and Collective Actions.e: Farida started with five friends and reached over two hundred volunteers within a year, urging action “however small”.

Individual and Collective Actions.q: Which word in the text means “a strong will to finish a task”?
o: concentration
participation
determination
responsibility
Individual and Collective Actions.e: Ms. Karim said she had never seen so much determination from young Egyptians.

Individual and Collective Actions.q: Omar said, “My team has designed a heater.” Report his words.
o: Omar said that my team has already designed a heater.
Omar said that his team has design a heater.
Omar said that his team had designed a heater.
Omar said that his team designing a heater.
Individual and Collective Actions.e: In reported speech, the present perfect usually moves back to the past perfect, and pronouns change.

Individual and Collective Actions.q: Farida said, “The river is changing rapidly.” Choose the correct reported sentence.
o: Farida warned that the river is changed rapidly.
Farida warned that the river were changing rapidly.
Farida warned that the river was changing rapidly.
Farida warned that the river has changing rapidly.
Individual and Collective Actions.e: In reported speech the present continuous moves back to the past continuous; “river” is singular, so “was changing”.

A World We Borrow.q: Why can no single country protect a migratory bird species alone?
o: Birds never stop during their long journeys.
Every wetland belongs to the same country.
Migratory birds only live in Egypt.
Birds depend on wetlands in many countries.
A World We Borrow.e: A wetland preserved in one country does not help a bird that starves during a stopover in another.

A World We Borrow.q: According to the text, what often happens to funding for wetland conservation?
o: It increases every single year.
It is always stable and fully protected.
It is paid by birdwatchers only.
It is cut first when budgets tighten.
A World We Borrow.e: Funding for wetland conservation is frequently the first thing cut when budgets tighten.

o: having the water removed
a short stop on a journey
extremely surprising in scale
making sure people follow rules
A World We Borrow.e: Staggering means extremely impressive or surprising in scale.

A World We Borrow.q: “We will lose our income,” the farmers said. Choose the correct reported sentence.
o: The farmers said that we will surely lose our income.
The farmers said that they will lost their income.
The farmers said that they would lose their income.
The farmers said that they would lost their income.
A World We Borrow.e: In reported speech, “will” moves back to “would”, and pronouns change to match the reporter.

A World We Borrow.q: Wetlands bring local communities both value and tension because they offer ecotourism income but are also …
o: protected by every country
owned by local birdwatchers
closed to visitors all year
wanted for development
A World We Borrow.e: Ecotourism can provide real income, yet the same flat, well-irrigated land is often wanted for development, so the pressures compete.

o: She asked where I was going.
She asked me where was I going.
She asked where did I go.
She said where am I going.
A World We Borrow.e: In reported questions, we use statement word order (subject before verb).

o: plants growing in an area
moving safely between two habitats
illegal hunting of wild animals
continuing for a long time
When Needs Compete.e: Poaching is the illegal hunting or capturing of wild animals.

When Needs Compete.q: Why does the lesson suggest that neither side is simply “right” in the conflict over land?
o: Both sides have genuine needs.
Elephants are not really endangered at all.
Grace has other ways to earn money.
Farmers never lose any crops.
When Needs Compete.e: Conservationists must protect endangered elephants, but Grace’s farm is her family’s only income; both needs are legitimate.

When Needs Compete.q: Complete: “The crops died because of a ……… drought that lasted for two whole years.”
o: legitimate
uninvited
trampled
prolonged
When Needs Compete.e: Prolonged means continuing for a long time; a drought lasting two years is prolonged.

When Needs Compete.q: Why is Grace’s view in the lesson a genuine concern?
o: She wants to hunt the elephants for money.
Her farm is her family’s only income.
She owns the wildlife reserve.
She has never seen an elephant.
When Needs Compete.e: Grace’s farm is her family’s only income, and elephant visits can destroy it.

When Needs Compete.q: How should you end a formal email to someone whose name you do not know?
o: Yours sincerely,
See you soon,
Yours faithfully,
With love from me,
When Needs Compete.e: The lesson says “Yours faithfully” is for an unknown name and “Yours sincerely” for a named person.

When Needs Compete.q: Which is a suitable opening for a formal email?
o: I am writing to request your support.
Hey! Guess what I want from you guys today?
Hi mate, hope you’re doing great!
So, here’s the thing, listen up.
When Needs Compete.e: Formal emails use polite phrases such as “I am writing to…” or “I am writing on behalf of…”.

Voices for the Voiceless.q: What motivated Nour to start her campaign?
o: finding a dead turtle in a fishing net
reading an article about sharks
a school project on marine life
a request from a group of local fishermen
Voices for the Voiceless.e: At fifteen she found a sea turtle tangled in a discarded fishing net near Hurghada; it had died.

Voices for the Voiceless.q: Several fishermen told Nour, “Fishing is our livelihood, not a hobby.” Choose the correct reported sentence.
o: They told her that fishing was their livelihood.
They told her that fishing were their livelihood.
They told her that fishing is our livelihood.
They said her that fishing was their livelihood.
Voices for the Voiceless.e: Reported speech backshifts “is” to “was” and changes “our” to “their”; “say” cannot be followed directly by a person.

Voices for the Voiceless.q: Why were some local fishermen not welcoming at first?
o: They did not like the beach at all.
They wanted to organize cleanups themselves.
Fishing was their livelihood, not a hobby.
They had already changed their nets.
Voices for the Voiceless.e: Several told her fishing was their livelihood and switching equipment was costly.

Voices for the Voiceless.q: What compromise did Nour’s campaign offer fishermen?
o: a complete ban on fishing near Hurghada
a fund for safer net attachments
free fish for every family
new boats from local hotels
Voices for the Voiceless.e: A small donation-based fund helps cover the cost of safer net attachments for willing fishermen.

Voices for the Voiceless.q: What does the writer mean by saying Nour is trying to fill “the gap”?
o: She repairs holes in old fishing nets.
She speaks for turtles that cannot speak.
She fills empty beaches with tourists.
She replaces fishermen who quit their jobs.
Voices for the Voiceless.e: Marine biologists note that turtles cannot speak for themselves or lobby a government; Nour speaks up for them.

Voices for the Voiceless.q: In the post, “Share before this gets banned! Tag someone NOW” is an example of …
o: hedging language
neutral language
urgency signals
clear evidence
Voices for the Voiceless.e: Urgency signals create pressure to act immediately.

Global Citizens, Local Actions.q: According to @GreenStepsEG, what did volunteers plant along the Red Sea coast?
o: 500 mangrove saplings
50 palm trees
5,000 olive trees inland
500 coral pieces
Global Citizens, Local Actions.e: Volunteers planted 500 mangrove saplings to protect the shoreline and provide nursery habitats.

Global Citizens, Local Actions.q: How did the GreenStepsEG project begin?
o: as a government coastal program
as a coastal hotel’s tourism project
as a large international campaign
as one student’s university project
Global Citizens, Local Actions.e: It began as a single marine biology student’s university project, then grew into a partnership with schools.

Global Citizens, Local Actions.q: How does the @GreenStepsEG thread show more than “good intentions”?
o: It asks everyone to save the whole planet.
It uses emotional words and urgency.
It reports specific, measurable results.
It was written by a government office.
Global Citizens, Local Actions.e: The thread gives measurable results, such as 500 mangrove saplings planted and early signs of reduced coastal erosion.

Global Citizens, Local Actions.q: Which of these is a measurable result of a local project?
o: 500 saplings planted in a weekend
We care very deeply about our beautiful sea
Everyone should help to save the planet now
Our project feels extremely important to us
Global Citizens, Local Actions.e: Measurable means able to be judged by a clear standard; a number of saplings can be counted, while feelings and appeals cannot.

Global Citizens, Local Actions.q: Complete: “No single volunteer can restore the coastline ………; it takes a whole community.”
o: indefinitely
enthusiastically
abstractly
single-handedly
Global Citizens, Local Actions.e: Single-handedly means without any help from anyone else, which contrasts with “it takes a whole community”.

Global Citizens, Local Actions.q: Why can global environmental problems cause a feeling of “paralysis”?
o: They are far too easy for one person to solve.
They only affect people in other countries.
They seem too enormous for one person.
They are only discussed by scientists.
Global Citizens, Local Actions.e: The lesson says global problems can feel too enormous for any individual action to matter, so people feel unable to act.

Consolidation Review C.q: “Solar power sometimes suffers from intermittency.” The opposite of “intermittency” is …
o: continuity
irregularity
interruption
variability
Consolidation Review C.e: Intermittency means stopping and starting, so its opposite is continuity.

Consolidation Review C.q: Complete: “Farida said that she ……… a Nile clean-up campaign with five friends.”
o: start
had started
has been start
will start
Consolidation Review C.e: In reported speech, the past action moves back to the past perfect: had started.

Consolidation Review C.q: In “A Planet with No Borders”, the writer mentions wildlife corridors in paragraph 3 mainly to …
o: explain how highways and roads are built
describe a practical solution
compare different species of large cats
argue that farms should be removed
Consolidation Review C.e: Paragraph 3 begins “To address this problem”, presenting corridors as a practical solution to habitat fragmentation.

Consolidation Review C.q: Which heading best fits paragraph 5 of “A Planet with No Borders”?
o: Why Every City Should Stop Growing Now
How Animals Behave Around Large Rivers
Building New Roads Across Thick Forests
Technology Supporting Conservation
Consolidation Review C.e: Paragraph 5 describes satellite tracking, motion-sensitive cameras and drones used to monitor animals and plan new corridors.

Consolidation Review C.q: According to “A Planet with No Borders”, habitat fragmentation causes wildlife to …
o: adapt to city life
reproduce more
become isolated
migrate every year
Consolidation Review C.e: Fragmentation divides ecosystems, so species may become isolated, reducing genetic diversity.

Consolidation Review C.q: What are wildlife corridors, according to the text?
o: busy highways built straight through thick forests
protected strips joining separated habitats
farms that keep wild animals out
zoos for endangered animals
Consolidation Review C.e: Wildlife corridors are protected strips of land that connect separated habitats.

From Hobby to Opportunity.q: How old was Mariam when she started decorating cakes?
o: sixteen
seventeen
nineteen
thirteen
From Hobby to Opportunity.e: At thirteen, she spent Friday afternoons piping wonky flowers onto cupcakes.

From Hobby to Opportunity.q: How did Mariam’s hobby turn into a business?
o: She made a full business plan first.
She kept saying yes to small requests.
Her parents opened a shop for her.
She won a big national baking contest on TV.
From Hobby to Opportunity.e: It was a slow accumulation of small moments; she kept saying yes to the next small request.

From Hobby to Opportunity.q: Why does Mariam keep one cake a month entirely unpaid?
o: to keep the joy of her hobby
to advertise to new customers
to practise for a competition
to give it to her teacher
From Hobby to Opportunity.e: Turning a hobby into paid work can drain the joy, so she keeps one cake just for herself.

o: a slow, gradual buildup of something
a narrow part of a pipe
to remove the enjoyment
not perfectly shaped or steady
From Hobby to Opportunity.e: Wonky means not perfectly shaped or steady, like her early piped flowers.

From Hobby to Opportunity.q: Complete: “She ……… bake only for fun; now she bakes for customers too.”
o: uses to
is used to
use to
used to
From Hobby to Opportunity.e: “Used to + verb” describes a past habit that is no longer true.

o: I didn’t used to show my drawings.
I didn’t use to showing my drawings.
I didn’t use to show my drawings.
I wasn’t use to show my drawings.
From Hobby to Opportunity.e: The negative form is “didn’t use to + verb”.

o: a book that records events and activities over time
a part that moves a bicycle chain between gears
a rule everyone knows but never writes
the quality of giving help freely
Building a Community Around Your Passion.e: A derailleur is the mechanism on a bicycle that moves the chain between gears.

Building a Community Around Your Passion.q: After years in a garage with no care at all, the old bicycle was in ……… .
o: disrepair
generosity
a logbook
obsession
Building a Community Around Your Passion.e: Disrepair means very damaged or in poor condition because of neglect, like a bicycle left without care.

Building a Community Around Your Passion.q: Youssef talks about bicycles all day and can hardly think of anything else. He is ……… with them.
o: generous
unwritten
obsessed
sustained
Building a Community Around Your Passion.e: Obsessed means thinking about something so much that it is difficult to think about anything else.

o: a personal diary entry about your private feelings
a short story with a surprise ending
formal writing recommending action on a problem
an informal message to a close friend
Building a Community Around Your Passion.e: A proposal identifies a problem and recommends a clear course of action.

Building a Community Around Your Passion.q: Which sentence belongs in “The Problem” section of a proposal?
o: It is recommended that a repair club meet weekly.
Currently, many students have no club to join.
The purpose of this proposal is to suggest a club.
We therefore urge the council to approve this plan.
Building a Community Around Your Passion.e: “Currently, many students…” introduces the problem; the others suit the Recommendation, Introduction and Conclusion sections.

Building a Community Around Your Passion.q: The meetups were “the only place where a specific, slightly unusual interest did not need explaining or defending.” This suggests members felt …
o: pressured to compete with one another
judged by strangers for their hobby
too embarrassed to talk about bikes
understood and accepted
Building a Community Around Your Passion.e: If an interest needs no explaining or defending, members feel understood and accepted rather than judged.

Leaving Your Mark.q: How did Hassan start his free chess lessons?
o: with twelve brand-new boards donated by the youth center
with one borrowed board and six mismatched pieces
with a paid course at a large chess club
with an online chess program for children
Leaving Your Mark.e: He began in the corner of a youth center with a single borrowed board and six mismatched pieces.

Leaving Your Mark.q: Why did most of the twelve children come in the first week?
o: Their parents forced them to come.
They were all chess champions.
Their school gave them extra marks.
A poster promised free snacks.
Leaving Your Mark.e: Twelve children came mostly because a poster promised free snacks as well as chess.

Leaving Your Mark.q: How did teaching change Hassan’s own understanding of chess?
o: He started to dislike playing chess.
He forgot many of the rules.
He understood the game more deeply.
He stopped playing chess alone.
Leaving Your Mark.e: Explaining strategies to children forced him to understand chess more deeply than playing alone.

o: The children would ask him blunt questions.
The children would to ask him blunt questions.
The children used ask him blunt questions.
The children were use to ask him blunt questions.
Leaving Your Mark.e: “Would + base verb” describes repeated past actions; “would to”, “used ask” and “were use to ask” are incorrect forms.

Leaving Your Mark.q: Why does the writer say that what Hassan left behind is “harder to put on a certificate”?
o: He won too many trophies to list them all.
It is a lasting club, not a prize.
The youth center lost all his records.
He never actually taught any lessons.
Leaving Your Mark.e: The club earned him no money or official credit; his legacy is a room still full most weeks, “still teaching itself forward”.

Leaving Your Mark.q: In the post, “If I can do it, literally anyone can” is an example of …
o: absolute language
hedging language
careful, sourced evidence
neutral language
Leaving Your Mark.e: Absolute language makes claims with no qualification or evidence.

Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.q: In the @SideQuestEG survey, how much time did students spend weekly on a hobby on average?
o: about 20 hours
about 10 hours
just 3 hours
just 30 minutes
Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.e: The average answer was just 3 hours, yet 90% said it was their favorite part of the week.

Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.q: How much time does Salma spend most evenings on her comic?
o: 2 hours or more
20 minutes
15 minutes
5 hours
Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.e: Salma spends 20 minutes most evenings on a comic she has been drawing for two years.

o: Working many hours just once is always the best way.
Talent matters more than any practice.
Regular small efforts beat rare big efforts.
A hobby should be finished quickly.
Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.e: Doing something regularly over time is more effective than putting in great energy occasionally.

Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.q: Yara practiced the piano for five hours every day for a month, then felt so exhausted that she stopped completely. She experienced …
o: deliberate practice
a sustainable habit
burnout
work-life balance
Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.e: Burnout is physical or mental exhaustion caused by prolonged stress or overwork, like Yara’s five-hour days.

Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.q: Which is the best example of deliberate practice?
o: playing favorite songs without any particular aim
watching a long concert online with friends
repeating one hard chord until it is clean
buying an expensive new guitar to feel inspired
Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.e: Deliberate practice is focused, intentional effort aimed at improving a specific skill, such as one difficult chord.

Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.q: In the @SideQuestEG survey, students spent just 3 hours a week on a hobby, yet 90% called it their favorite part of the week. What does this suggest?
o: Students have no free time for any hobbies.
A little hobby time can matter a lot.
Hobbies need more than 20 hours a week.
Most students dislike their hobbies.
Time Well Spent: Balancing Passion and P.e: Although the time was small, most students valued it highly, which supports the idea that consistency matters more than intensity.

Vocational Education in Egypt.q: Why is vocational education important for young people in Egypt, according to the lesson?
o: It replaces all school subjects with sport.
It focuses only on theory and exams.
It prepares students to live abroad.
